newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition portrays itself as pro-West.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition portrays itself as pro-West.

text.p: The opposition coalition leading street protests in Serbia this week supports democratic reforms and post-war reconciliation but some of its leaders have flirted with nationalist ideology for political gain.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition, which accuses the ruling Socialists of massive poll fraud, is comprised of three parties unified by their opposition to President Slobodan Milosevic's authoritarian rule.

The parties, the Democratic Party (DS), the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), and the Civic Alliance (GSS), have formed a loose alliance supporting political and free-market reforms and an end to what they call Milosevic's "dictatorship".
Opposition leaders sharply disagree with Western diplomacy that treats Milosevic and his autocratic counterpart in Croatia, President Franjo Tudjman, as pillars of Balkan stability.
The opposition argues the West should recognise that stability cannot come to the region without the sort of fundamental change that swept through the rest of Eastern Europe seven years ago.
"It goes without saying that this (democratic) transformation cannot be carried out by the political forces which provoked and conducted the war...", says a policy statement issed by Zajedno.
The youthful, clean-cut leader of the Democratic Party, Zoran Djindjic, now rivals the flamboyant writer Vuk Draskovic as the main opposition leader.
Djindjic was touted to become the first non-communist mayor of the capital Belgrade since World War Two until the ruling Socialists annulled poll results.
Djindjic, who earned a doctorate in philosophy in Germany, leads a party that sells itself as pro-Western and includes prominent independent economists.
Draskovic, with his long hair and soaring oratory, led a similar wave of street protests in 1991 which Milosevic crushed with tanks and water-cannons.
Draskovic is still greeted as a hero among many demonstrators but his critics within the coalition say his often romantic approach to politics lacks discipline.
A former journalist and novelist, he was once a hardline nationalist in communist-ruled Yugoslavia. He switched course after war broke out in Croatia, warning that the conflict was a useless tragedy.
Milosevic, unlike other communist party leaders in the old East bloc, managed to hang on to power by championing Serb nationalism in former Yugoslavia.

He was widely blamed for plunging the country into four years of bloodshed. But as the tide of war turned against the Serbs, Milosevic recast himself as "peacemaker" and signed a peace treaty last year.
Djindjic's party, which includes some genuine nationalists, has pursued contacts with the ultra-nationalist Bosnian Serb leaders who fell out with Milosevic's "peace policy".
Earlier this year, Djindjic himself appeared at a major campaign rally of the ruling Bosnian Serb party, a gesture that plays well among some voters but makes Western diplomats wary.
Political analysts say the opposition's mixed messages about nationalism merely reflect confusion and contradictions in Serbian society about it views the Yugoslav conflict.

The opposition leaders say they hope to use the protests to present the coalition as a coherent alternative to Milosevic. But they remain deeply divided, barely able to agree on tactics for daily protests.
"The coalition needs to be developing detailed policies and still has to settle this balancing act between liberals and nationalists," said one opposition adviser.
